Leading the way to Old Madam Xia's courtyard, Qianli Xun had Hongdou wait outside the gate with the storyteller while she walked in alone.
Maids were supporting Old Madam Xia on a slow stroll around the yard. Catching sight of her granddaughter-in-law, the old lady snapped, "What dreadful manners! Barging in without being announced—and you call yourself the Poetess of Jiangnan!"
Any pep talk Qianli Xun had given herself to mimic Chen Haoyu's breezy charm evaporated on the spot. "As the Poetess of Jiangnan, I have a broad heart, Grandmother. If the sight of me grates on you, I won't take offense. Today I brought someone to liven up this quiet courtyard."
Ignoring the old lady's glare, Qianli Xun started directing the maids. "You two, carry a table out here. You, fetch a chair."
Seeing Old Madam Xia keep silent despite her frown, the maids realized she did not object and hopped to work.
Once the table and chair were set, Qianli Xun stepped forward to take her arm. "However annoyed you are with me, Grandmother, set your anger aside for today and let me help you sit."
Watching her granddaughter-in-law bustle around and stir up the sleepy courtyard warmed the old lady inside, though her mouth stayed sharp. "Fine, I'll sit and see what trick you have up your sleeve."
Once Old Madam Xia was seated, Qianli Xun called toward the gate, "Hongdou, bring in the storyteller!"
At the word "storyteller," Old Madam Xia could no longer keep up her scowl; the corners of her mouth quirked upward. Catching that tiny smile out of the corner of her eye, Qianli Xun grinned inside: Hooked already! Life in Chen Manor is about to get smooth sailing.
Hongdou escorted the storyteller in. Feeling right at home at the sight of the table, he walked over, pulled his wooden clapper and folding fan from his cloth satchel, set out his purple clay teapot, and told a nearby maid, "Be a dear and brew me a pot of tea."
Old Madam Xia's smile broadened. "Brew the gentleman our finest tea."
The maid hurried off with the pot. Old Madam Xia glanced at Qianli Xun standing beside her. "Have a seat too." Another maid scurried off for a chair.
Sitting down, Qianli Xun said, "Grandmother, he tells tales written by Master Qianli Xun. You're sure to love them."
"You went to a lot of trouble." Old Madam Xia's voice had softened by half.
When the teapot arrived, the storyteller took a sip—rich flavor, warm without scalding. Satisfied, he set the pot down and launched into his preamble. "Who in Lin'an doesn't know the splendor of Chen Manor, overflowing with fortune and honor, and Old Madam Xia blessed with longevity and noble virtue..."
Old Madam Xia cut him off with a laugh. "Enough flattery. Get straight to the story! Tell it well, and I won't skimp on the reward."
"Say no more, Old Madam—your wish is my command!" He slapped the wooden clapper onto the table with a sharp crack.
"Now, at the southern edge of heaven stood a Glazed Pagoda, trapping a jade-faced fox for a full thousand years. That fox did not sit idle: she made the pagoda her home, fed on its mist, dressed in its dust, and grew every bit as pagoda-bound and quirky as the tower itself..."
Old Madam Xia burst out laughing. "Ha! First time I've ever heard a fox called 'pagoda-quirky'—hilarious!"
The storyteller rolled right on. "At the southern edge of heaven also dwelt a high immortal named Xuanzhi. Every day after cultivation, he stared at the Glazed Pagoda. A true deity with blazing eyes full of divine power, he poured his gaze into that tower day after day until the pagoda absorbed more power than it could hold. One day, with an earth-shaking BOOM, the Glazed Pagoda shattered to pieces! Freed at last, the jade-faced fox caught a drift of immortal aura and took human shape as a maiden—though after a millennium inside a dusty tower, she stood grimy and disheveled from head to toe.
"Just then the deity Xuanzhi appeared. Startled, the maiden blurted out, 'Who are you? Decent face, though you look sour enough to curdle milk.'
"Xuanzhi swept his sleeve; every speck of dust vanished, revealing a stunning beauty. 'I saved you,' he declared. 'From now on, you belong to me.'
"Glad as she was to look gorgeous, his arrogance set her fuming. 'Who says you saved me? I didn't see a thing!' She turned to bolt, only for Xuanzhi to reel her straight back with a flick of immortal power..."
Old Madam Xia laughed till her sides shook. Not since her sons had married and set up separate quarters had anyone brought her this much joy.
Before long, news of a storyteller performing in Old Madam Xia's yard spread through the manor. Chen Haofei came running to listen, followed by Second Aunt Madam Bao, Third Aunt Madam Cui, and Ye Anya. The courtyard buzzed with laughter, leaving Old Madam Xia beaming from ear to ear.
#CH 217
#TITLE: Reading an Elder's Mind
After the storyteller finished and departed, Old Madam Xia leaned back in pure contentment and issued her next order. "Once isn't enough! Have him come every single day."
"Rest assured, Grandmother," Qianli Xun replied. "I already arranged for him to come at this exact hour every day to tell you stories."
The old lady grinned until her eyes vanished into creases.
Second Aunt Madam Bao piped up in a vinegary tone, "Who would've guessed Haoyu's bride is even better at coaxing Old Madam Xia than Haoyu himself? I envy First Sister-in-law for landing such a clever daughter-in-law—unlike the one in my house..." She shot a hard glare at Ye Anya beside her. "Learn a thing or two from Shuzhen! Otherwise what good did it do Haodong to marry you?"
Ye Anya kept her head bowed and endured her mother-in-law's scolding in silence. Old Madam Xia frowned in displeasure yet held her peace.
Qianli Xun stayed quiet and watched. Having binged plenty of household-intrigue dramas before her transmigration, she knew inner-courtyard politics could not be solved with fists; they took brains. Madam Cui and her son Chen Haofei stayed out of it too, long used to watching Ye Anya get berated.
Madam Bao was not done. "Can't blame my Haodong, though—he's busy dawn till dusk running the silk shop, tea house, salt store, porcelain firm, wharves, inns, and restaurants. Not like Haoyu and his wife, with endless free time to butter up Old Madam Xia. Don't favor one grandson and forget the other, Mother, or Haodong will be heartbroken."
Hearing the barbed jab, Old Madam Xia's smile dropped dead. "Save your reminders. I have my own scales in my head. Who has character, who has ability, and who contributes to the Chen family—every bit is clear as glass to me."
Not to be outdone after Madam Bao sang her son's praises, Madam Cui jumped in. "My Haofei can't match either of his older cousins—one schemes well, the other knows how to play and please his grandmother. All my boy thinks about is his books. Next year he sits for the metropolitan exam, and if he passes, he goes straight to Bianliang for the palace exam! Haofei, recite a passage from the Erya for your grandmother."
"Never mind," Old Madam Xia waved a hand. "I wouldn't understand it even if he recited it. Haofei is a good lad. Study hard and bring home an imperial title for the Chen family—that will be the greatest contribution of all."
"Yes, Grandmother," Chen Haofei answered.
"All of you run along now," Old Madam Xia ordered. "I want a private word with Haoyu's wife."
Watching the crowd file out and replaying the two aunts' speeches, Qianli Xun understood at last why Old Madam Xia doted on Chen Haoyu despite all his flaws—he was the one grandson who came just to make her laugh without waving ledgers or ambition in her face.
Once the yard emptied, Old Madam Xia spoke. "Shuzhen, help me inside."
Supporting her up, Qianli Xun felt how stiff and weak the old lady's legs were. Thinking of the Old Ancestor back at Zhu Manor—a hundred and twenty years old and spryer by miles—a wave of pity and fondness hit her. "Grandmother, Chen Haoyu mentioned a physician who treats leg ailments. I'll track him down for you another day."
Old Madam Xia laughed. "You believed Haoyu? He just says that to cheer me up. The Chen family has silver to burn—what doctor couldn't we hire? We brought them all in years ago. Nobody can cure these legs."
Puzzled, Qianli Xun helped her onto the kang couch, slipped off her own shoes, and sat cross-legged across from her. "So you aren't angry with me anymore, Grandmother?"
Old Madam Xia chuckled. "When was I ever angry with you?"
Qianli Xun froze a second, then gasped. "You were pretending to be mad at me the whole time? Had I known that, I wouldn't have racked my brains trying to win you over!"
"At last I've found someone in Chen Manor with a working head," Old Madam Xia said. "Picking fights and acting mad was just my way of getting you to pay attention and coax me—yet none of my sons or daughters-in-law ever caught on."
Everything clicked into place for Qianli Xun. Every time Old Madam Xia snapped and groused at Chen Haoyu's parents, she was only fishing for affection and company, only to push them further away. Qianli Xun had stumbled onto the right answer by sheer luck.
"You ought to tell your sons and grandchildren what you like straight out, Grandmother."
Old Madam Xia sighed. "Where's the fun if I have to spell it out? Anyone who cares about me will figure it out on their own—just like you put real thought into making me happy. From today on, you're under my wing in Chen Manor. Nobody dares lay a finger on you."
Qianli Xun teased her. "Since I married in, nobody besides you has tried to bully me, Grandmother—and even if they did, my fists aren't for show."
"Oh, listen to you brag!" Old Madam Xia laughed, her eyes crinkling. "Still, that's what I like about you—afraid of nothing under heaven, just like me in my youth. Pity I've grown old."
"Wait—are you pulling my leg, Grandmother?" Qianli Xun asked, half thrilled and half skeptical. "When I stormed over here before the wedding, you looked ready to skin me alive! And during the tea ceremony too—how could you have liked me?"
"The day you came raising a ruckus, anyone could see you didn't want to marry Haoyu. Why would I force it? With you putting on a show like that, wouldn't smiling back have ruined your act? Besides, I worried you'd actually beat up my grandson after the wedding, so I played along to help torpedo the match."
Qianli Xun marveled at how deep Old Madam Xia ran—one face on the surface, a whole different mind underneath. No wonder her sons and daughters-in-law stayed baffled.
Recalling that pre-wedding clash reminded Qianli Xun of a slip the old lady had made back then. "Grandmother, that day you said my father forced Chen Haoyu to marry me. Why did he do that?"
Old Madam Xia's guard snapped up at once. Her granddaughter-in-law still did not know, meaning Prefect Zhu had kept it from her on purpose. She cursed her own loose tongue from that day. With Shuzhen's temper and fists, spilling the secret now would spell doom for Haoyu.
"Nothing of the sort! You had me so flustered that day I spouted nonsense. Don't think twice about it."
Spotting nothing off in the old lady's expression, Qianli Xun let it drop. "Grandmother, how did you like Master Qianli Xun's story?"
"Wonderful! Best tale I've heard—never heard anything so fresh!" Old Madam Xia praised, then paused with a sharp look. "Though you called the author a male scholar. Funny—it sounded like a young woman wrote it."
Thrilled by the praise—the last sting of her pre-transmigration cyberbullying melted away—Qianli Xun also marveled at the old woman's sharp instincts. "What makes you say that?"
"A story about a young girl's heart? Had to be written by a girl."
Qianli Xun rattled off a smooth defense. "Not so fast, Grandmother! In the Tang dynasty, the Poet Immortal Li Bai wrote 'Qingping Yue,' the Poet Sage Du Fu wrote 'A Fair Lady,' and the Poet Buddha Wang Wei wrote 'Ballad of the Daughter of Luoyang.' All about women, yet every last one was a full-grown man."
Delighted by her granddaughter-in-law's learning, Old Madam Xia wondered what mountains of merit her book-hating grandson had piled up in a past life to land a literary genius. "Spoken like the Poetess of Jiangnan! You know everything."
Buoyed by the compliment, Qianli Xun thought of another treat. "Grandmother, I know an old blind drummer who sings drum ballads. Another day I'll invite him over to sing the tale of Cai Bojie for you."
Old Madam Xia bobbed her head like a pellet drum. "Yes, yes, yes!"
The two talked and laughed until noon approached and the old lady needed lunch.
Barely a few paces outside Old Madam Xia's courtyard with Hongdou, Qianli Xun found her path blocked by Chen Haofei. "Greetings, Second Sister-in-law!"
"Third Brother," Qianli Xun said, recognizing him from earlier. "Something I can help you with?"
"I have a favor to beg of you, Second Sister-in-law. You must say yes!"
Unfamiliar with him, Qianli Xun stayed cautious. "Tell me what it is first, then I'll decide."
"I passed the provincial exam, yet my poetry is weak and I have no name in Lin'an. Whenever I get invited to poetry salons, I just sit in the corner with nothing new to offer. Now that the renowned Youqi Jushi is my sister-in-law, could you spare me a poem or two so I can shine at salons? Please?"
Spreading Zhu Shuzhen's poetry? Qianli Xun never turned that down. "I thought it was something tough. Jotting down a couple of poems is easy. Come ask whenever you want."
"I'd love them right now!"
"Then follow me."
Beaming, Chen Haofei trailed her back to Moxiang Courtyard. At the gate, they spotted Ye Anya waiting alone.
"First Sister-in-law, why are you standing out here without even a maid?" Qianli Xun called out.
"I was waiting to chat with you, Sister," Ye Anya said. "What brings Haofei here?"
"Greetings, First Sister-in-law," Chen Haofei said. "Second Sister-in-law promised me two poems, so I tagged along."
Ye Anya smiled. "Having the famous Youqi Jushi marry into the Chen family sure gave you a leg up! No more showing up empty-handed to salons."
"Of course—we're family now!" Chen Haofei grinned.
Chatting and laughing, they entered Moxiang Courtyard. Kuqiao had already laid out lunch, yet Qianli Xun sat down at her desk first to write for Chen Haofei. Since it was spring, she penned two seasonal ci lyrics: "Xijiang Yue: Mid-Spring" and "Dielianhua: Seeing Spring Off." Chen Haofei accepted the fresh sheets with profuse thanks and bounced off on air.
Since it was lunchtime, Qianli Xun invited Ye Anya to stay and eat. Ye Anya accepted; having waited at the door till noon, declining would have been awkward.
They sat down to four dishes, a soup, and rice. By now Qianli Xun had grown used to Song meals; what intrigued her was why her sister-in-law had sought her out.
Kuqiao ladled soup and stood ready to serve.
"First Sister-in-law, you're the only woman near my age in Chen Manor," Qianli Xun said. "We ought to visit each other often."
Ye Anya sipped her soup. "I had the exact same thought, which is why I came over today."
Qianli Xun placed a serving of vegetables into Ye Anya's bowl. "I'm brand new here and don't know the ropes yet. Whenever you have time, fill me in so I don't say the wrong thing or upset the elders."
"Word is you never wanted to marry into the Chen family," Ye Anya observed. "You didn't consummate the marriage on your wedding night, and you don't care where Haoyu roams—yet you go out of your way to please the elders. I can't quite figure you out."
"I didn't want to marry Chen Haoyu, true, yet fate boxed me in. Now that I'm here, I treat myself as part of the Chen family and mean to live here in peace."
Those words—"fate boxed me in"—reminded Ye Anya of Prince Yi raiding the wedding procession. Even a prince had wanted this woman; why had the Zhus refused a prince and handed her to a rake like Haoyu?
"Outsiders think you and I struck gold marrying into the Chen household," Ye Anya sighed. "Only we know the bitter taste inside. Haoyu stays out day and night, and my own husband may look better on the surface, yet..."
She broke off. Catching the ache in her tone, Qianli Xun put another morsel in her bowl. "Try this dish—it's pretty good."
Ye Anya ate a bite, then went on. "I envy you, Sister. You're fierce and know your own mind—you took over Haoyu's property and remade this courtyard just the way you like it. Whereas I..."
"I only got away with that because Father and Mother-in-law are generous, the elders indulge me, and I have a sister-in-law willing to speak from the heart with me."
Ye Anya let out a startled laugh. "What a honeyed tongue! No wonder you won Old Madam Xia over so fast. I heard how she marched over with my mother-in-law and Third Aunt to pick a fight, and you argued them so flat they walked off speechless. That mouth of yours spins poetry and sharp logic alike!"
"You flatter me, First Sister-in-law."
Laughing and chatting over lunch, Qianli Xun felt the warmth of a big, bustling household—flawed only by having married the wrong man. If only Chen Haoyu were the man she loved.
That thought pulled Shen Jianchen straight into her head. He and Mengrong must still be on the road to Bianliang. By the time they came back to Lin'an, everyone would call Mengrong Princess Consort Yi.
In silence, Qianli Xun sent up a quiet wish that Prince Yi and his new princess consort would find happiness together.
#CH 218
#TITLE: Poor, Pitiful Ye Anya
After lunch and another long chat at Moxiang Courtyard, Ye Anya tore herself away with reluctance.
Beyond being close in age, Ye Anya felt drawn to her new sister-in-law by curiosity and awe. Obtaining a mutual divorce already left most women stunned; enduring citywide slander the year before while living with zest would have driven an ordinary lady to jump into the Qiantang River ten times over. Engaged to Haoyu, she had ditched all gentlewoman airs to storm Chen Manor and wreck the match—failing, yes, yet showing jaw-dropping nerve. And on her wedding day, Prince Yi himself had raided her bridal procession, leaving Princess Jiahe wounded—proof that even on the brink of marriage, a man could still love her with reckless passion.
Today had been their first real talk, so Ye Anya had kept her deepest question to herself. She had watched and listened, hoping some of Shuzhen's steel would rub off on her and give her the nerve to do what she had long yearned to do yet feared. She resolved to visit Shuzhen often.
Back in her own courtyard, Ye Anya found her mother-in-law Madam Bao waiting with a face like thunder.
Ye Anya curtsied at once. "Mother, what brings you here?"
"Midday, and instead of eating in your own quarters, you come wandering home past the meal hour! Where were you gallivanting?"
The word "gallivanting" stung, yet Ye Anya forced a smile. "'Gallivanting' is harsh, Mother. I only went to chat with Shuzhen. She pressed me to stay for lunch, and I couldn't refuse."
"Hmph!" Madam Bao snapped. "Look at Shuzhen—married in only days ago, and Old Madam Xia already eats out of her hand! And look at you—over two years here, and how many times have you visited Old Madam Xia, let alone won her over for Haodong? And that belly of yours—still flat as a board! No wonder Haodong can't stand you and hates coming back to this courtyard!"
Too weary to endure more berating, Ye Anya said, "If you have nothing else, Mother, I'll go inside." Without waiting for leave, she walked into her room.
Madam Bao bristled and turned to her maid. "Look at that! Does she act like a meek daughter-in-law? And outsiders praise her as gentle and filial, making me look like the wicked mother-in-law!" With a sharp huff, she marched off.
Inside, Ye Anya lay across her bed, choking down silent resentment.
Her maid Xiaocui hurried over. "Miss, I checked our usual spot this morning. Young Master Cao sent a note."
Ye Anya sat up at once, snatched the folded slip from Xiaocui's hand, and read the Han ballad inked inside:
"O Heaven! I would be with you, / And my love will never die. / Only when mountains are gone, / And all rivers are dry, / When thunders roll in winter, / In summer snowflakes fly, / When heaven and earth join as one, / Only then my love may die!" [TN: Translated by Zhang Longxi]
Ye Anya sighed. "He gives me his whole heart, yet I'm another man's wife. How can I ever honor a love like this?"
"You and Young Master Cao loved each other first, Miss," Xiaocui whispered. "You were forced to marry Young Master Chen. The way he beats and curses you—even if you can bear living like this, I can't bear watching it."
"I can't bear it either. Yet the wedding is done. What choice do I have?"
"Didn't you want a mutual divorce, Miss?"
"I do—yet walking that road isn't simple."
"The Zhu lady just married in, and she went through a mutual divorce. Why not ask her how she did it?"
"That's the very reason I visited her today, yet the words stuck in my throat. Next time I'll find a chance to ask."
Just then Chen Haodong strode through the door. Xiaocui whipped the note from her mistress's fingers, stuffed it up her sleeve, and shrank to the side.
Chen Haodong glared at the maid. "Getting ruder by the day—don't even know how to greet your master?"
"Greetings, Young Master," Xiaocui stammered.
Ye Anya rose from the bed. "You're back early today, Husband."
"What, annoyed I came back early? Hiding someone in here you shouldn't be? Don't think I don't know about your little affair with the Cao boy before we wed."
Fragile yet stubborn, Ye Anya held her chin up. "Whatever passed between us is in the past, and you knew before we married—why dredge it up now? Since you're bringing up dirt, let's talk about Chun Jinchan. Don't think I haven't heard about the filth you get up to with her outside."
Knowing what came next, Xiaocui went rigid with terror.
"Get out!" Chen Haodong roared at Xiaocui.
Xiaocui dropped to her knees. "Young Master, please don't beat Miss! Her bruises from last time haven't even healed!"
"Guards!" Chen Haodong shouted toward the door. Two manservants rushed in. "Drag Xiaocui outside and shut the door!"
They obeyed at once. Once the door clicked shut behind them, Chen Haodong stalked toward Ye Anya. "Getting bolder by the day. Looks like I went too easy on you last time."
Ye Anya backed away. "Think beating me will make me submit? You're wrong. Every blow only makes me despise you more!"
Chen Haodong grabbed her collar. "Mother just told me you've been cozying up to Haoyu's wife! Listen good: don't pick up her habits. Her name is mud across Lin'an. You keep your spotless reputation intact—next year the clan names the heir to the Chen fortune, and you'd better not ruin my shot!"
Ye Anya refused to swallow her scorn. "You put on a noble act for outsiders, yet I know what filth you really are. A man like you inheriting the Chen estate—"
Crack! His palm smashed across her cheek. "Shut your mouth!"
Blow after blow rained down until Ye Anya lost the strength to resist. He hurled her onto the bed and tore at her clothes. "Beating you first and making you do your wifely duty after—nothing feels better!"
Sick with humiliation yet powerless to stop him, Ye Anya could only clench her teeth and endure.
When he finished, Chen Haodong straightened his robes and sneered down at his bruised, weeping, disheveled wife. "Cold as a block of ice in bed—no wonder you can't get pregnant! You should take lessons from the courtesans at Chunxiang Brothel on how to please a man."
Only after the door slammed shut did Ye Anya let her tears spill.
Xiaocui hurried back in and broke down at the sight of her mistress. "Miss, next time just humor him and don't talk back—you're the only one who ends up hurt."
"I can't humor a man I loathe. Giving in kills my soul; I'd rather take bruises on my skin than rot inside. I'm leaving him—even if he writes me a bill of divorce and casts me out, I'm ending this marriage."
Seeing a steel in her mistress's eyes she had never witnessed before, Xiaocui felt a fierce relief. Ye Anya had not known a single happy day in Chen Manor; leaving—even alone and shamed—beat living in this hell.
Over the following days, the storyteller came to Chen Manor every afternoon, turning Old Madam Xia's once-lonely yard into the liveliest spot in the house. Yet Ye Anya never reappeared. Still new to the household, Qianli Xun thought it unwise to pry or drop by uninvited, so she held back.
She noticed Yao Qingyan and Chen Jianglin stayed absent too. One afternoon, while Old Madam Xia and the crowd sat rapt by the story, Qianli Xun slipped out—and spotted Yao Qingyan pacing beneath a tree near the gate with her maid Yingxue.
Qianli Xun walked over. "Mother, you're right at the gate. Why aren't you going in?"
"I'm afraid seeing me will only upset Old Madam Xia," Yao Qingyan admitted.
Her in-laws were good people who simply could not read the old lady's heart, trapped in years of needless friction. Time to lend a hand.
"You're overthinking it, Mother," Qianli Xun said. "Grandmother craves lively company. If you fill her courtyard with warmth and chatter every day, she'll beam—why would she get mad at you?"
Yao Qingyan looked doubtful. "Will that really work?"
"Worked like a charm for me! Look how she laughs nonstop now and treats me like a different person."
"How did you read her mind right after arriving, when I've been her daughter-in-law for decades and never noticed she craved company?"
"Not my genius—Matron Wei pointed it out to me."
"No wonder every young lady in Lin'an envies you for having Matron Wei."
Qianli Xun took the chance to flatter her. "What Lin'an envies most is how devoted Father is to you."
Yao Qingyan chuckled, then clouded over again. "Everyone admires our devotion—everyone except Old Madam Xia, who seems to resent it."
"Did you ever wonder, Mother," Qianli Xun prompted, "if Grandmother's anger at you and Father has nothing to do with your bond, and everything to do with something else?"
"Something else? I can't imagine what."
"Only after I cheered her up did I find out: whenever she snaps and acts angry, she isn't mad at all. She's acting up to grab attention, hoping we'll put thought into cheering her up so she won't feel lonely."
Light broke across Yao Qingyan's face. "So that's it! No wonder the harder Jianglin and I tried, the more she scolded us—and the more she scolded, the more we stayed away! Why couldn't she just say so instead of letting us misunderstand her all these years?"
"She told me spelling it out spoils the fun. She wants to feel someone cares enough to figure it out on their own. Old folks are just like kids—they want to feel noticed and cherished. From now on, if you and Father stop by every day to keep her courtyard lively, I guarantee she'll be thrilled."
"Now I see why she dotes on Haoyu—not just because he looks like his late grandfather, yet also because he drops by her room to sweet-talk her!" Yao Qingyan gripped Qianli Xun's hand. "Shuzhen, the Chen family made the best choice of all bringing you in. Barely through the door, and you untangled a knot that baffled us for years. Thank you."
Your Chen family chose right—I'm the one who got the raw deal! Qianli Xun thought, smiling aloud instead. "Don't just stand out here talking. Come inside with me. Grandmother is in high spirits right now; she won't get mad."
Yao Qingyan nodded and stepped inside with her. The storyteller was in full swing:
"Xuanzhi gave the jade-faced fox a name—Luoying—and made her a maid in his celestial palace, serving his meals and tea every day. All heaven revered Xuanzhi for his boundless power; even the Heavenly Sovereign showed him respect. Yet Luoying looked down her nose at him—cold as stone, never cracking a smile, boring to tears!
"Every day after chores, Luoying lingered beside the lotus pond talking to a single lotus blossom. One afternoon she sighed to the flower, 'Oh lotus, serving that icy god is dull as dirt. I want to sneak out of his palace and roam somewhere fun.'
"Suddenly a voice answered, 'I'll take you.'
"Luoying jumped in fright. 'Who said that?' Looking around, she saw no one. Rising from her stone to flee, she spun around and came face to face with a dazzlingly handsome young man.
"She stepped back. 'Who are you?'
"'I'm the lotus blossom who listens to you every day,' the youth smiled. 'Just call me Flower Prettyboy.'
"Luoying burst out laughing. 'What a cheesy name!'"
Absorbed in the tale, Old Madam Xia did not notice her eldest daughter-in-law enter. Without disturbing her, Yao Qingyan walked up behind the old lady's chair. Qianli Xun offered her own seat, yet Yao Qingyan shook her head, waving away a chair a maid brought too. Standing behind Old Madam Xia, she rested her hands on the old woman's shoulders and began kneading them while listening to the story.
Feeling her touch, Old Madam Xia turned her head, saw Yao Qingyan, and said not a word—yet her smile deepened with warm satisfaction.
A boulder lifted from Yao Qingyan's chest. At last she knew how to make her mother-in-law happy, and she could not wait to tell Jianglin tonight.
Watching from the side, Madam Bao sneered inside: Hmph! Look at First Sister-in-law buttering up the old lady! Madam Cui felt a pinch of annoyance too, yet shrugged it off and went back to the story.
#CH 219
#TITLE: First Sister-in-Law's Secret
Once the storyteller wrapped up and left, the younger generation drifted out too. With Haofei absent today, Madam Cui worried over her son and excused herself. Seeing Yao Qingyan stay behind, Madam Bao lingered as well, unwilling to let her eldest sister-in-law hog Old Madam Xia's favor. Knowing Yao Qingyan had heart-to-heart words to share, Qianli Xun bowed out.
The two daughters-in-law helped Old Madam Xia indoors. The old lady glowed with joy: her courtyard buzzed again, her eldest daughter-in-law had caught on, her eldest son would soon follow, and lonely days were over.
The moment Old Madam Xia settled on the couch, Yao Qingyan dropped to her knees. "Mother, I was wrong all these years to misread your heart. Beat me or scold me however you please."
Before Old Madam Xia could speak, Madam Bao grumbled, "If Sister kneels like that, how am I supposed to sit?"
Ignoring Madam Bao, Old Madam Xia reached for Yao Qingyan. "Get up. Just drop by my yard when you're free to keep me company. Don't leave me sitting alone until I have to pick fights just to get your attention."
"Yes, Mother," Yao Qingyan promised. "I'll come sit with you every day from now on." Yingxue helped her up into a chair.
"Honestly, Mother, you should have just told us!" Madam Bao chimed in. "I'll have Haodong and his father come keep you company every day, and I'll come too."
"Don't stand there—sit down," Old Madam Xia said. "So long as you keep me in your hearts, I'm happy."
Surrounded by two attentive daughters-in-law, a rare treat indeed, Old Madam Xia beamed nonstop.
Having won Old Madam Xia over lifted a huge weight off Qianli Xun's shoulders. On paper she had everything: property, a custom courtyard, the matriarch on her side, kind in-laws, and a friendly sister-in-law in Ye Anya. Yet deep down, an ache refused to lift.
In a subdued mood, she jotted down an address and handed the slip to Hongdou. "This is Xiaguo's old family home. Go invite her grandfather to Lin'an whenever he has time—tell him Chen Manor's old madam wants to hear him sing drum ballads."
Hongdou hurried off, leaving the room hushed. Wondering idly where Kuqiao had gone, Qianli Xun sat still and examined the emptiness inside her chest until the answer stood plain: she had no one beside her whom she loved.
Thoughts of Shen Jianchen surfaced at once. By now he must be nearing Bianliang. She sighed at her crooked path in love, cursing an era where a person could not even choose their own heart's match.
Kuqiao walked in and spotted her mistress propping her chin on her hand, looking glum. "What are you thinking about, Miss?"
Skipping the question, Qianli Xun asked, "Where have you been?"
"With the storyteller here, I dared not show my face outside, so I stayed in the West Courtyard watching Qinggua practice."
Qianli Xun lowered her hand. "Hardly martial arts—just one self-defense move I taught him out of pity because Chen Haoyu keeps kicking him. How's he doing?"
"With Asheng sparring with him, he's starting to look sharp—much smoother and faster than when you showed him."
Not in the mood to talk about Qinggua's drills, Qianli Xun stood. "I want to go see the Divine Willow."
Recognizing her mistress's low mood, Kuqiao asked no questions and followed her out to the carriage.
Kuqiao had never quite grasped why both her mistress and Prince Yi kept returning to that tree. Bai Feng had told her Prince Yi wandered out from Youlin Retreat to sit beneath it all the time, muttering as if the willow could understand human speech.
Mid-thought, Kuqiao glanced out the carriage window and spotted Huayu and Nan Shuang walking together toward Chen Manor. "Miss, I just saw Huayu and Nan Shuang! Think they're heading to Chen Manor to ask for your poems?"
Qianli Xun ordered the driver to halt. "Call them over."
Kuqiao poked her head out. "Nan Shuang! Huayu! Over here!"
Both servants trotted over to the carriage.
"How did you two run into each other?" Kuqiao asked.
"My master told me to visit Chen Manor every few days from now on to ask for Youqi Jushi's poems," Nan Shuang explained. "Ran straight into Huayu on the road, and it turns out he's on the same errand."
"Come to think of it, you haven't come asking since Young Master Qiao got back from Bianliang," Kuqiao remarked. "Miss is heading out right now, so come by tomorrow. Don't worry—she already wrote plenty, waiting on her desk."
Huayu panicked at once. "Those are all for my master, right? You can't cut our share just because Nan Shuang showed up!"
"Miss writes poems fast and brilliant," Kuqiao assured him. "Seven or eight sheets are already sitting on her desk. Your share won't shrink, and there's plenty left for Nan Shuang too."
Delighted, both servants saw the Chen carriage roll on.
Qianli Xun had listened to every word in silence. Now she spoke. "Nan Shuang used to come asking for my poems before?"
"Hardly asking—just hovering around to scavenge spoiled drafts you tossed out."
"Why did he stop once Wenyuan came back from Bianliang?"
Kuqiao eyed her mistress with care. "Think about it, Miss. You'll know."
The prompt hit home. When Wenyuan returned from Bianliang, she had fallen for him at first sight; once they had each other's love, who needed poems as a bridge? Then their romance hit rocks, leaving him in no mood for verse, and after their breakup beneath the Divine Willow, less still. Sending Nan Shuang now meant Wenyuan had healed at last—that final meeting at Zuiyun Tower had closed their chapter clean.
A soft smile curved Qianli Xun's lips. Funny how love worked: walking into it brought joy, and walking cleanly out of it could bring relief too.
Then her smile faded. Walking into feelings for Shen Jianchen had never brought her joy—only guilt, as if a single flicker of gladness made her immoral. When would this chapter close clean for both of them? Every time she tried to draw a full stop in her heart, her hand stopped halfway. Why punish herself so hard? Couldn't she at least keep the man she loved tucked quiet inside her heart? Torn as ever, she left him right there.
Outside the city gates, the carriage reached the foot of the hills. Qianli Xun stepped down and walked toward the Divine Willow. Spring breezes brushed drifting willow catkins across her face, scattering white, feather-light fluff across the path.
Up close, the tree wore two colors now: if the red ribbons dressed the Divine Willow in a bridal gown, the drifting white catkins draped a bride's veil over its boughs. The mashup of ancient and modern imagery amused her; an ancient willow that bridged a thousand years would surely forgive the anachronism.
Over the pond, young lotus leaves unfurled beneath a thin dusting of willow fluff, with bare patches of water coated white as well. Too poetic a scene to waste Zhu Shuzhen's brush—Qianli Xun recited aloud:
"Whirling through clear skies like flying snow, / Drifting high, unwilling to touch the mud. / Soft beside blossoms, clinging to bees' wings; / Reckless on lanes, chasing horses' hooves. / Flat on the water, turning to duckweed borne far by waves; / Playing on the wind, shadowless, skimming low walls. / Gathering in clusters, grieving that spring must go, / Longing to cloud the road of the departing Spring God." [TN: Translator's rendering of Zhu Shuzhen's "Willow Catkins"]
Kuqiao clapped her hands. "Marvelous, Miss! Especially 'clinging to bees' wings'—so lifelike! I just saw a bee foraging on that wildflower get snagged by a puff of fluff on the petal, beating its wings forever before shaking loose!"
Qianli Xun smiled. That praise belonged to Zhu Shuzhen's razor-sharp eye for life. All at once a truth struck her: whether classical poets writing verse or modern web novelists spinning tales, both lived or died by observing real life. Looking back, she had drawn online outrage before her transmigration because her later books drifted further and further from reality. Adapting huaben in this era, she would weave in the texture of Song life—even in tales of gods and immortals, listeners should hear their own lives reflected back.
Yet writing was not why she had come. Spotting the boulder beneath the willow, she walked over, bent down, and blew away its coat of white fluff. Fearing the stone would chill her mistress, Kuqiao spread a silk handkerchief over it and stepped back to stand guard.
Qianli Xun sat down and leaned her back against the rough trunk. Though she had never seen him do it, she pictured Shen Jianchen sitting on this exact stone, listening to his own heart. Thinking of Bai Feng trying to train a pig to climb this trunk brought a mix of tenderness and laughter.
After a pause, she opened her eyes. "Kuqiao, did you know Bai Feng was training a piglet to climb the Divine Willow?"
"Bai Feng told me," Kuqiao said. "Prince Yi had him buy a piglet and try teaching it to climb. Heaven knows what His Highness was thinking—pigs climbing trees! Sounds absurd just hearing it."
"Absurd indeed. He wanted to turn the impossible into the possible, refusing to see that impossible stays impossible—pouring out all that stubborn effort for nothing." Closing her eyes again, she sank back into quiet melancholy.
Kuqiao caught the hidden weight in her sigh; no one knew the tangle between her mistress and Prince Yi better than she did.
Qianli Xun dared not pray to the Divine Willow for romance—any prayer for Shen Jianchen felt like a knife aimed at Mengrong. She would lock her feelings deep inside and live out her days as a dutiful daughter-in-law in Chen Manor.
After a long spell, growing stiff, she stood to leave with Kuqiao.
Barely a few steps down the path, a man and woman emerged from the back slope. Qianli Xun recognized the man first—Young Master Cao Ban—and almost stepped out to say hello until she saw the woman holding a red silk ribbon beside him with a radiant face: her First Sister-in-law, Ye Anya.
Startled, Qianli Xun aborted the greeting and pulled Kuqiao behind a thick tree trunk to peer back toward the willow.
Hand in hand, Cao Ban and Ye Anya stepped beneath the Divine Willow, knotted their red ribbon onto a bough together, and fell into a tight embrace, looking every inch a match made in heaven.
"Miss," Kuqiao breathed, "if Eldest Young Master Chen finds out, First Young Madam is finished."
"There's bound to be a reason behind this," Qianli Xun warned in a whisper. "Remember: take what we saw today to your grave. Never breathe a word to anyone."
"Yes, Miss. My lips are sealed."
Before the pair noticed them, Qianli Xun hurried away with Kuqiao.
Her own tangled feelings faded beside her pity for Ye Anya. She was far from the only woman trapped in this era, barred from the man she loved—there were countless Zhu Shuzhens and Ye Anyas. How she missed the modern world! Taking freedom for granted had blinded her to its worth; living without it showed how precious a thousand years of struggle had been. Since she could never go back, she would cherish what she could hold here: family—her living parents, brother, sister-in-law, the one-hundred-and-twenty-year-old Old Ancestor, plus Grandmother Xia and her fair-minded in-laws—and friendship: the three salon scholars, Wenyuan as a confidant, Xiangrong, and Mengrong.
Remembering Mengrong brought back the slap on her wedding day and those words of hatred. Even so, Qianli Xun bore Mengrong no grudge. No matter how Mengrong treated her from now on, she would remain Qianli Xun's one true best friend in this era.
#CH 220
#TITLE: Three Elders Plot Who Holds the Reins
When Chen Jianglin returned from the silk shop, Yao Qingyan told him everything that had happened that afternoon. Realization hit him hard: he had misread his mother for decades, talking big about filial piety while missing the heart of it.
He took Yao Qingyan straight back to Old Madam Xia's courtyard. Having left only a short while ago, Yao Qingyan did not mind the extra trip one bit; now that the old lady greeted her with warm smiles, visiting felt like a pleasure.
Anticipating her eldest son's arrival, Old Madam Xia sat on her couch flipping through a poetry volume, picking out Shuzhen's verses and frowning. "Why are Shuzhen's poems all steeped in grief when her personality is nothing like that?"
A maid at her elbow answered, "Old Madam knows what Young Madam went through before marrying into the Chen family. After trials like that, how could anyone stay cheerful?"
Old Madam Xia nodded. "True enough. Anyone in her shoes would hurt. Now that she's in Chen Manor, things will brighten bit by bit."
Just then Chen Jianglin and Yao Qingyan entered. Old Madam Xia laid the book aside. "Back already? Tiring day?"
Chen Jianglin lit up—the first warm greeting from his mother since Wenxin was born. He drew Yao Qingyan forward to bow. "Working for the family is never tiring, Mother."
Before Yao Qingyan could bend her knees, Old Madam Xia waved her off. "My daughter-in-law already paid her respects today. Come sit across from me, Qingyan—make him do the bowing."
Yao Qingyan straightened up without hesitation and took the seat opposite. Chen Jianglin completed his bow, sat in a side chair, and waited for his mother to speak.
"You two landed a fine daughter-in-law, and I landed a fine granddaughter-in-law," Old Madam Xia said. "If she hadn't taken the trouble to read my heart, you two might never have figured out what I wanted."
"Forgive your unfilial son, Mother," Chen Jianglin said. "I failed to understand your heart and misjudged you for years. Thanks to Shuzhen, she solved it the moment she arrived—which shames me all the more for missing something so simple as head of the household."
"Stop beating yourself up. Just come sit with me often and keep this yard lively, and I'll be content enough to live a few extra years."
"Whenever business allows, Qingyan and I will come keep you company every day, Mother. Keep you smiling, and you'll live to a hundred."
Laughter rippled around the room, before Old Madam Xia sighed. "We're all sorted out, yet my grandson is still roaming outside day and night—hasn't even consummated his marriage yet. We can't let this drag on."
Emboldened by their newfound warmth, Yao Qingyan spoke up. "If neither you nor I step in to stop him, the second Haoyu comes home, let Jianglin give him a proper thrashing and lock him up so he can't run wild!"
Instead of bristling, Old Madam Xia blamed herself. "I spoiled Haoyu because he looks just like his late grandfather, and because back when you two didn't understand me, only Haoyu knew how to coax a laugh out of me. Every time Jianglin tried to discipline him, I flew off the handle and stopped him. Looking back, I ruined the boy."
Yao Qingyan owned her share too. "Not all on you, Mother. I worried Jianglin would beat him too hard and kept shielding him myself."
Chen Jianglin grinned. "So you both agree to let me come down hard on the brat?"
"My own suggestion—of course I agree!" Yao Qingyan declared. "Punish him however you see fit; I won't lift a finger to stop you."
Old Madam Xia smiled with a knowing glint. "I don't think the three of us will even get a turn."
Yao Qingyan caught on at once. "You mean Shuzhen?"
"Exactly," Old Madam Xia nodded. "Nobody better for the job."
"Before, Qingyan and I asked Shuzhen to handle him only because she wasn't scared of you stepping in," Chen Jianglin pointed out. "Now that we're all on the same page and you agree to let me discipline him, why burden Shuzhen?"
"Sounds logical, yet leaving Haoyu to Shuzhen has three huge perks," Old Madam Xia counted off. "First, I already handed her the job—can't take it back now. Second, the three of us get to kick back and relax. Third, and most important, when Shuzhen disciplines Haoyu, they'll rub elbows nonstop. Knock two stones together long enough, and sparks are bound to fly!"
Chen Jianglin clapped his knee at that third reason. "Brilliant as ever, Mother. Done deal."
Yao Qingyan frowned with worry. "Only Shuzhen signed that prenuptial contract promising not to meddle in each other's lives. We told her to rein him in, yet she brushed it off—Haoyu's been gone for days and she hasn't batted an eye, spending all her time entertaining you."
Old Madam Xia winced in guilt. "My fault. The afternoon they came back from Zhu Manor, he came coaxing me because he was broke, and I caved and handed him a five-hundred-tael note. That's why he vanished again."
Chen Jianglin smiled and broke it down for her. "Don't blame yourself, Mother. That actually proves Shuzhen already has him on a leash! Steward Fang told me Haoyu went to Xinglong Pavilion to draw silver, and Steward Fang demanded a written order from Shuzhen. Haoyu didn't dare ask her for one, which is why he ran crying to you."
"Handing his properties over to Shuzhen was the right move after all!" Yao Qingyan cheered.
"She's starting by controlling his purse strings," Old Madam Xia chuckled. "Give her time and she'll whip him right into shape."
"Just don't slip him any more silver, Mother!" Yao Qingyan reminded her.
"Never again, never again!"
Right then Chen Jiangshu and Chen Jiangmu walked in together. Tipped off by their wives about Old Madam Xia's craving for company, neither brother wanted the eldest to monopolize her favor; bumping into each other outside the gate, they came in side by side, greeted their mother and eldest brother, and took seats.
"Mother, whatever you want from now on, don't keep it bottled up making us guess," Chen Jiangshu began. "Just say the word—which of us three would dare refuse?"
"Right, Mother!" Chen Jiangmu echoed. "We're busy running Chen enterprises all day and we're clumsy men—how are we supposed to guess the subtle thoughts in your head?"
On any other day, grumbling like that would have triggered a lecture, yet Old Madam Xia was in too fine a mood to care. "When you three were babies who couldn't talk, I spent over a year guessing every little thing each of you wanted! Now I ask you to guess my mind once, and you complain?"
All three brothers chorused, "We're glad to guess, Mother!"
Old Madam Xia turned first to her second son. "You raised Haodong into a sharp businessman, which gladdens me, yet you forgot to teach him how to treat his wife. When you three married, I drilled into every one of you to cherish your wives, and you all did well. Why didn't you pass that down to your own son? Word reached me that Haodong beats Anya all the time."
"Rest assured, Mother," Chen Jiangshu replied. "I'll give Haodong a stern talking-to tonight and make him treat Anya better."
Next she addressed her third son. "Haofei is a good lad, buried in his books. If he earns an imperial degree, our ancestors will beam from their graves. Still, he can't stay nose-deep in pages forever—holding office means dealing with people. Knowing how to converse and read folks can't be learned from books alone."
"Well said, Mother," Chen Jiangmu answered. "I'll guide him. Actually he's made real strides lately—Second Sister-in-law gifted him several poems, and he's been beaming, heading out to poetry salons every few days to mingle with scholars and exam candidates."
Old Madam Xia nodded, more certain than ever that bringing Shuzhen into the house had been a stroke of genius. After more family banter, the old lady tired, and everyone excused themselves.
Walking back to their quarters, Yao Qingyan asked, "Should we send men out to haul Haoyu home?"
"He runs off all the time," Chen Jianglin said. "We never chased him before, no need to start now. Once his silver runs dry, he'll crawl home on his own—then we back Shuzhen up while she straightens him out."
Seven or eight days slipped by. Small lotus pads broke the surface of Moxiang Courtyard's pond and fanned out, breathing fresh life into the yard. Between sitting with Old Madam Xia and writing huaben, Qianli Xun barely gave Chen Haoyu a passing thought, living as though she had moved into Chen Manor solely as a cherished daughter and granddaughter. Only when Yao Qingyan or Old Madam Xia asked if Haoyu had come home did she remember she was married to a man she despised.
Whenever the elders urged her to drag him back and discipline him, Qianli Xun nodded on the surface while balking inside. The Chens were wonderful folks, only they overestimated her willingness—why waste energy reforming a wastrel like Chen Haoyu? Sensing her lack of enthusiasm, the elders dropped the subject, though the quiet disappointment on their faces gave her a twinge of guilt.
Over those same seven or eight days, Master Jiang's wounds healed enough for him to handle gang affairs—and remember Chen Haoyu. Figuring the brat was still haunting Chunxiang Brothel for Chun Jinmo, he marched straight into the brothel with five thugs in tow. He kept the squad small on purpose: bringing a mob last time had drawn Commandant Lin and gained him nothing, and he had no desire to tangle with the garrison again.
Even with five men, Master Jiang's swagger commanded every eye in the hall.
The madam rushed over. "Welcome, Master Jiang! Right this way!"
Settling into a table, Master Jiang leered up at Chun Jinmo dancing on stage. "Once her dance ends, send her down to pour wine for me."
The madam pulled an apologetic face. "I'm afraid I can't, Master Jiang—Young Master Chen booked her exclusive."
Master Jiang stood and strode straight to Chen Haoyu's table.
Chen Haoyu had already clocked him. Seeing only five thugs while his own three bodyguards sat nearby, he stayed lounging in his chair, admiring Chun Jinmo's dance without a flicker of worry.
Master Jiang dropped into a chair opposite him. "Still hanging around Chun Jinmo, Young Master Chen?"
With his promissory note ashes in the wind, Chen Haoyu had zero fear left. "Heh! All that grand gambling scheme of yours flopped, didn't it? Sure I married a tigress, yet I have a knack for taming wildcats! She's sweet as a kitten now—never clips my wings, purrs at me all day, lets me roam wherever I please. Jealous?"
Master Jiang's jaw tightened. "Chen Haoyu, hand Chun Jinmo over right now, or I'll knock every tooth out of your head!"
At his sharp look, his five thugs closed in. Paid to keep trouble off their patron, the three hired bodyguards stepped in to block them.
Patrons scattered to safety while Chun Jinmo froze mid-dance on stage, watching with anxious eyes. Upstairs, Scarface and his cronies leaned over the railing from a courtesan's balcony to gawk.
"Another brawl," one lackey muttered.
"Next chance we get, we ought to talk Young Master Chen into dropping Chun Jinmo," another said. "Plenty of prettier girls in Chunxiang Brothel."
"What do you know?" Scarface scoffed. "Young Master Chen is devoted—hates switching women."
"Devoted? First time I've heard that word used in a brothel!"
"Shut up and watch the fight!"
Downstairs, fists flew. Chen Haoyu and Master Jiang stayed seated across from each other, trading sneers.
"Level with me," Chen Haoyu prodded. "What did Prefect Zhu pay you to rig that trap and force me to marry his leftover daughter?"
Master Jiang never saw that guess coming—and saw a golden chance to spin a yarn and scare the boy off Chun Jinmo. "Sharp as a tack, Young Master Chen! You guessed it! I run the underworld, sure, yet I have backers in the yamen—Prefect Zhu himself! Who else would I help? He ordered me to whip you into shape and warn you to stay out of Chunxiang Brothel and stay home with his daughter, or else!"
Chen Haoyu shot to his feet in fury. "Big deal, so he's the Prefect! Sticking his nose into my private life? I'll come here every single day just to drive him crazy!"
Before he could swear further, he spotted his three bodyguards gaining the upper hand, and his anger melted into gloating. "Look at your pathetic thugs—getting wiped across the floor by my three guards! Hahaha!"
Seeing his five men pushed back and refusing to lose face in public, Master Jiang stood and barked, "Stop!"
Both sides broke apart. Master Jiang jabbed a finger at Chen Haoyu. "I'll let you off today! Next time you won't be so lucky!" Then he shouted toward the stage, "Chun Jinmo! Sooner or later you're mine!"
Turning to the three bodyguards, he gave a thumbs-up. "Nice moves, boys. The Qiantang Gang's doors are always open to you. See you around!"
#CH 221
#TITLE: Eldest Cousin Plays His Trump Card
Having taken a hit to his pride, Master Jiang needed someone to pay the tab—and Chen Haodong was top of the list.
The eldest Chen cousin had roped him into a convoluted scheme that accomplished nothing: Chen Haoyu was not reined in by his fierce bride, and Master Jiang had been made a fool of. The silver Chen Haodong had paid did not come close to soothing his bruised dignity.
Busy at the silk shop—where booming trade with the southwest kept him tied down every day—Chen Haodong looked up as a gang of men barged through the door, scattering the shopkeeper and clerks in terror.
Recognizing Master Jiang's stormy face, Chen Haodong hurried forward. "What brings you here in person, Master Jiang?"
"If you don't want the whole world knowing what you cooked up, take me somewhere private," Master Jiang growled.
Guessing the reason at once, Chen Haodong led him into the back warehouse. Part of Master Jiang's crew guarded the door while the rest followed inside.
The storeroom reeked of sharp dye and stacked bolts of silk. The instant the door shut, Master Jiang skipped small talk and waved his men in. With no martial training, Chen Haodong could only curl up and take the beating.
When he figured it was enough, Master Jiang barked, "Stop!"
Wincing through his bruises, Chen Haodong gasped, "Barging in and beating me without a single word—is that any way to do business?"
"A beating is getting off light!" Master Jiang snarled. "You conned me into rigging that wager to make Chen Haoyu marry a tigress, swearing she'd lock him down so he'd leave Chun Jinmo alone! Instead she doesn't lift a finger, he's still living it up with Chun Jinmo every day, and I just ate dirt trying to take him on!"
"Even so, I paid you every tael I promised. You didn't lose out."
"Your paltry silver doesn't begin to cover my face and aggravation!"
"I want that fierce bride locking Haoyu down just as bad as you do," Chen Haodong panted. "I didn't foresee her signing a prenuptial contract to stay out of each other's hair. Still, I have one trump card left. Give me a few days, Master Jiang, and Chun Jinmo is all yours."
Master Jiang crouched beside him. "Not stringing me along again?"
Chen Haodong crooked a finger. "Lean in and I'll tell you."
Master Jiang tilted an ear down while Chen Haodong whispered a few rapid sentences. A wide grin spread across Master Jiang's face. "So Chen Haoyu was behind that! All right—I'll trust you one more time."
With a nod, Master Jiang had a lackey toss a vial of salve into Chen Haodong's lap and led his men out.
Pocketing the medicine, Chen Haodong hauled himself up, warned the shopkeeper and clerks never to breathe a word to the Chen elders, and rode back to Chen Manor. The bruises were surface-deep; two days of rest put him mostly back on his feet.
Over those two days, he mulled over how to leak Haoyu's rumor-mongering to the Zhu girl.
A servant stepped in. "Eldest Young Master, Second Master is back and asks to see you."
A plan snapped into place. Chen Haodong beckoned the servant over, slipped a tael of silver into his palm, and said, "Take this. Pull this off and there's more waiting."
Delighted, the servant pocketed the coin while Chen Haodong murmured instructions in his ear. "Pass it along to the servants at Moxiang Courtyard today."
"Yes, Eldest Young Master."
Once the servant left, Chen Haodong stood to go see his father—only for Ye Anya to walk in with Xiaocui behind her.
One look at Ye Anya's cool, expressionless face set Chen Haodong's temper flaring. "Where have you been?"
"Out on the street buying rouge and powder."
"Hmph! When have you ever worn rouge for me? Sneaking out to meet your lover and dolling up for him?"
Hit dead center, Ye Anya felt a jolt of alarm yet kept her face stone calm. "If you have nothing else, I'm going to my room."
Since their wedding night, that icy detachment had driven him mad. He had assumed once he made her his woman, she would thaw, smile, and soften toward him. Instead, no matter how many times he forced himself on her, she stayed cold as marble.
Blocking her path, her aloofness stoked his urge to dominate. He seized her wrist and snapped at Xiaocui, "Get out!"
"Young Master, please don't!" Xiaocui cried.
"Get out!" he roared.
Too drained to fight back, Ye Anya spoke flat. "Go outside and shut the door, Xiaocui."
Xiaocui withdrew and pulled the door shut.
Yet Ye Anya's hollow compliance killed Chen Haodong's appetite. He flung her hand away. "Cold as a slab of stone in bed—I won't touch you again."
Ye Anya let out a silent breath, only for him to spin back at the door, seize her in his arms, and crush his mouth onto hers. Struggling for air, unable to push him off, she endured his bruising kiss until he pulled back, holding her tight.
"Chen men are supposed to treat their women well," he muttered. "Father keeps telling me to be kinder to you, yet the second I look at you, all I want is to conquer you. Can't you stop freezing me out? Maybe then I'd treat you better."
Ye Anya answered with dead silence.
He let go. "Father wants to see me."
The instant the door closed behind him, Ye Anya shuddered in disgust and scrubbed his touch off her lips with a silk handkerchief.
Meanwhile, the bribed servant hovered outside Moxiang Courtyard until Asheng walked out. "Asheng!"
Asheng halted. "What's up?"
Pulling him aside, the servant lowered his voice. "Got something huge to tell you—about your young madam and Second Young Master."
Asheng stayed wary. "They're fine. What about them?"
"Remember last year when the whole city was trashing your young madam's name?"
"Just people making up filth! Miss is nothing like that."
"Pity your young madam is still in the dark, clueless about who started those rumors."
"You heard who did it?"
"I've lived in Chen Manor for years—of course I know!"
"Spill it," Asheng urged, "so I can help Miss teach the blind bastard a lesson."
Glancing around to make sure the path was empty, the servant whispered, "It was the groom himself—Second Young Master Chen! Bet you never guessed your mistress married the very man who ruined her name."
Asheng gaped. "Where'd you hear that?"
"Overheard Second Master and Eldest Young Master talking. Sat so heavy on my chest I figured someone in Moxiang Courtyard ought to know, and ran straight into you. Feels better getting it off my chest. Gotta run!"
Frozen in place, Asheng reeled. If the shock staggered him, what would it do to Miss? Should he tell her or keep quiet? Deciding to finish his errand first, he hurried off with a spinning head.
Outside Chen Manor's main gate, a Qiao carriage drew up. Xiaguo stepped out first, followed by Aimo helping the old blind drummer down.
Taking her grandfather's arm, Xiaguo reminded him, "Grandfather, Miss married into the Chen family now. Call her Young Madam when we go in."
"You've drilled that into me ten times already—my ears are calloused!" the old man chuckled. "Is the Chen family as rich as the Qiaos?"
"In silver, the Chens are the richest family in Lin'an—the Qiaos can't touch them," Xiaguo explained. "In prestige, though, the Qiaos are imperial kin, and the Chens can't match that."
"Each has its own glory—worlds apart from country folk like us," the blind drummer said. "Just know your place in the Qiao household and live peaceful."
"So you aren't ashamed of me being a concubine anymore?"
"Made peace with it. What good is grumbling now that you're married? So long as you live well, your parents and I are glad."
"Come on, Grandfather. Miss must be waiting."
Having given the storyteller a day off for the blind drummer's visit, Qianli Xun was working on her huaben in Suxin Thatched Hall until a maid announced, "Concubine Xia of the Qiao household is here."
Setting down her brush, Qianli Xun had Kuqiao stow her drafts and went out to meet them.
Meeting them in the yard, she stepped forward to steady the old man. "Thank you for making the trip, Elder. Few singers left can perform drum ballads like yours, so I invited you to sing a tune for our old madam."
"Young Madam showed endless kindness to our Xiaguo," the old man replied. "At one word from you, this old bone comes running."
"Would you like to rest first, or head over to Grandmother's yard now?"
"Sat enough in the carriage—let's go sing for the old madam right away."
"Then I'll escort you."
"Miss," Xiaguo spoke up, "I'll wait here while you get Grandfather settled, so we can chat once you're back."
Qianli Xun nodded and called Hongdou over to host Xiaguo inside Suxin Thatched Hall before guiding the blind drummer out.
Stepping inside, Xiaguo looked around before sitting. "Why do the furniture and layout look identical to Wangyue Pavilion? Felt like I stepped right back into your old boudoir."
Measuring out tea powder at the tea table, Hongdou explained, "It looked nothing like this when Miss first arrived. She had everything redone to her liking and hauled all her old furniture over from Wangyue Pavilion."
"I see." Noticing Hongdou whisking tea, Xiaguo raised a brow. "You learned to make tea too?"
"Matron Wei had Sister Kuqiao teach me. She said Sister Kuqiao will marry Guard Bai sooner or later, so I should learn how to serve Miss up close."
Xiaguo settled on a cushion across from her. "Passable form, though you still need practice."
"I'm just starting out, still clumsy—though Miss says my tea tastes decent."
"Serving Miss brings good luck," Xiaguo mused with quiet pride. "Look at me: married into Qiao Manor as half a mistress, to the man I love. Even Kuqiao is set to marry Prince Yi's personal guard—beats marrying some rich household's footman! Know Youfan?"
"No."
"What about Nan Shuang?"
"Him I know—he came by yesterday to ask for Miss's poems for Young Master Qiao."
Xiaguo sniffed in disdain. "Youfan is Miao Zhiyu's maid. Nowhere near as lucky as us—Nan Shuang has her wrapped around his finger, and she's thrilled about it."
Hongdou set down the finished bowl. "Your tea, Concubine Xia."
Xiaguo took a sip. "Not bad at all." Turning to Aimo behind her, she instructed, "Once we're home, you learn to whisk tea too."
"Yes! Please teach me, Concubine Xia!" Aimo beamed.
"Of course. I can't match the tea masters at Yongtai Teahouse, yet I beat Kuqiao hands down—the pupil surpassed the teacher. Stay loyal to me, and I'll arrange a better match for you than that Youfan will ever get."
"Thank you, Concubine Xia!"
Right then Qianli Xun walked back in. "What's got you all so cheerful?"
Setting down her bowl, Xiaguo rose to greet her. "You're back, Miss! I have so much to tell you."
Qianli Xun already knew what was coming—endless Qiao Manor gossip she had zero interest in. Still, for the old blind drummer's sake, she could spare an hour to listen to Xiaguo chatter.
#CH 222
#TITLE: Dull Chatter with Xiaguo
Chatting with Xiaguo was bound to drag; sitting indoors without a view would make it twice as dull.
"Let's talk beneath the hehuan silk tree in the courtyard," Qianli Xun suggested.
Matron Wei had already placed a rattan chair and wooden table under its shade. Hongdou brought out an extra chair for Xiaguo, and Kuqiao set down a platter of seasonal fruit before stepping back to attend. With Kuqiao on duty, Hongdou slipped off to the West Courtyard to watch Qinggua drill; by now he had mastered seven or eight tenths of the Phantom Sidestep and stood a solid chance of dodging his master's kicks.
Though summer had not arrived, the midday sun was already sharp. Beneath the canopy, dappled light filtered through leaves without scorching delicate skin—a setup Xiaguo admired at once.
"I noticed this courtyard on your wedding day, Miss," Xiaguo praised as she sat. "If I recall right, there wasn't even a single tree back then. Look at it now—all your favorite chrysanthemums, lotus sprouting in the pond, and this lush hehuan tree. Anyone can tell at a glance who rules this roost."
"Chen Haoyu promised me this courtyard before we wed. Since it's my turf, I fixed it up to please my own eyes."
Xiaguo sighed. "Being primary wife beats everything. As a concubine in Qiao Manor, I could never dream of treatment like this."
"At least you married the man you love," Qianli Xun consoled her.
That hit the sweet spot. Formidable and sought after as Miss might be, she had ended up married to a man she did not want; by comparison, Xiaguo counted herself blessed. A shy smile lit her face. "There's something you ought to congratulate me on, Miss."
Leaning back in the rattan chair, eyes closed to savor the fresh leaf scent and warm flecks of sun, Qianli Xun asked, "What?"
"Wenyuan and I consummated our union," Xiaguo confessed, blushing.
Without opening her eyes, Qianli Xun smiled. "Telling me bedroom secrets to my face? No shame at all."
"I think of you as family, Miss—that's why I tell you. Wenyuan consummated his marriage with Miao Zhiyu too, keeping the bowl level. She's nicer to me on the surface now, though her words still carry needles."
With zero appetite for another family's domestic friction, Qianli Xun stayed silent.
"You don't know, Miss—Miao Zhiyu plays the refined lady outside, yet her heart isn't half so kind. Every few days she hunts up excuses to bully me. Good thing I'm no fool; Wenyuan sides with me more often than not, so she can't pin me down."
Obliged to answer, Qianli Xun kept her eyes shut. "Judging people is tricky—it all depends on where you stand. Attending salons with Miao Zhiyu, I found her gentle and gracious; during last year's rumors, she spoke up for me behind my back, so I thought well of her. How she is now, I can't say, since I don't live under her roof like you."
Taking that as validation, Xiaguo warmed to her theme. "Shared salon memories aside, she doesn't actually like you, Miss. Whenever Wenyuan sends Nan Shuang over every few days for your poems, Miao Zhiyu stews. Just yesterday she grilled Wenyuan right to his face, asking if he still can't let Youqi Jushi go..."
Surprised that a few of Zhu Shuzhen's verses were stirring trouble in Wenyuan's home, Qianli Xun opened her eyes and gazed across her garden, trying to tune out Xiaguo's chatter.
Xiaguo rattled right on. "Wenyuan said he's moved on, and I believe him, yet Miao Zhiyu doesn't. She ordered him to quit sending Nan Shuang for poems, and he refused! Of course I backed Wenyuan, so he's been spending most nights in my room lately. Miao Zhiyu fumes, and the madder she gets, the happier I am!"
Staring up at the new branches of the hehuan tree, picturing its pink blossoms, Qianli Xun wanted nothing more than to wrap this visit up. "Xiaguo, pass word to Wenyuan not to send Nan Shuang for poems anymore."
"No way!" Xiaguo balked. "That's Wenyuan's one joy. I won't ruin his mood."
"Then next time Nan Shuang comes, I just won't hand any over." Qianli Xun shut her eyes again.
"No way!" Xiaguo objected again. "Since when do you care what Miao Zhiyu thinks, Miss? Proves her love for your poetry was fake all along! Guess who she's thick as thieves with these days?"
On second thought, Qianli Xun realized Wenyuan was not the only scholar collecting her poems, yet no other household fought over them. The fault lay not in Zhu Shuzhen's verse, rather in petty hearts; if someone looked for offense, they would find it anywhere. Her conscience was clean—she shared Zhu Shuzhen's art, not private romance. Fine, she would leave it be.
Answering Xiaguo's prompt, she murmured one word: "Who?"
"Lin Jue's wife, Bai Meiruo!" Xiaguo grimaced at Lin Jue's name, remembering how he had once pawed at her and tied her up. "She drops by Qiao Manor to see Miao Zhiyu nonstop, and Miao Zhiyu introduces her around to her close friends. Something about Bai Meiruo rubs me wrong. Funny enough, Lin Jue's new concubine seems decent—only met her once, yet she struck me as alright."
Qianli Xun's eyes popped open. Barely ten days since her run-in with Bai Meiruo, and Lin Jue already had a concubine? "Don't tell me it's Chun Jinqiao from Chunxiang Brothel?"
"You heard already?" Xiaguo marveled. "News travels fast!"
Not news—I practically handed her the blueprint, Qianli Xun thought.
"Bai Meiruo may be awful, yet she treats Lin Jue well," Xiaguo went on. "She dipped into her own private dowry three days ago, bought Chun Jinqiao out of Chunxiang Brothel, and installed her as Lin Jue's concubine. Yesterday Miao Zhiyu dragged me to a banquet where every wife brought her concubine—thought she was being nice, turned out it was just a pack of primary wives tearing down concubines! That's where I met Chun Jinqiao."
Qianli Xun closed her eyes a third time to savor the spring breeze. "They actually throw banquets like that? Skip them from now on."
"Only went because I didn't know better—next time she asks, I'm refusing flat! Still, I met every big household's concubines there and learned they host private gatherings of their own. I joined right in, so now I have plenty of parties to attend!"
Xiaguo wore a smug, settled grin—she had found her tribe, a circle where concubines could trade stories and gripe about their primary wives.
With closed eyes, Qianli Xun quoted Laozi. "The old sage got it right: 'Good fortune lies within misfortune; misfortune lurks within good fortune.'"
Baffled by the proverb, Xiaguo searched for a reply just as a maid from Old Madam Xia's courtyard arrived to rescue both of them.
"Young Madam, the elder has finished singing, and Old Madam Xia wants to chat with him over lunch. She sent me to invite you and Concubine Xia to join them."
More than ready to escape inner-courtyard gossip, Qianli Xun rose from the rattan chair at once. "Come on, let's go eat at Grandmother's."
Lunch in Old Madam Xia's bustling courtyard spared Qianli Xun any more of Xiaguo's chatter. Afterward, Qianli Xun walked both guests out to the gate.
The blind drummer left loaded down with reward silver—enough to live comfortably for a full year without roaming dusty roads for coppers. Seated in the carriage, he marveled at the generosity of wealthy homes.
"Don't marvel over them, Grandfather," Xiaguo sniffed. "Even without Chen silver, what I send home is enough for everyone. Quit trudging village to village singing!"
"Your own path in Qiao Manor isn't easy," the old man cautioned. "Stop sending us everything—tuck silver aside for yourself so your spine stays stiff in that house. And remember: keep peace with your in-laws and primary wife. Harmony makes a household prosper."
"You've told me a dozen times, Grandfather. I remember."
Back in Moxiang Courtyard, Qianli Xun spotted Asheng pacing restlessly in the yard. "Asheng, need something?"
Asheng spun around, opened his mouth, hesitated, and blurted, "Nothing, Miss—heading to the West Courtyard to help Qinggua drill!" He bolted off like a man with a secret burning his pocket.
Qianli Xun frowned. "What's gotten into Asheng?"
"Word is Asheng has a crush on Hongdou," Kuqiao murmured. "Probably wanted to beg you to match them up."
Qianli Xun laughed. "He likes Hongdou? If he's too shy to speak up, let's pretend we noticed nothing." Thinking no more of it, she went back inside to write.
Halfway to the West Courtyard, Asheng collided with Hongdou. Bursting with the secret, he tugged her behind a wall.
"Hey, why are you dragging me?"
"I'm about to explode!"
Hongdou teased him. "Go use the latrine then—you'll feel better!"
"Not that kind of exploding! I'm holding a secret that's choking me!"
Long aware of Asheng's crush, Hongdou assumed he was about to confess, and heat rushed to her cheeks. "Go ahead—I'm listening."
Asheng leaned in. "Remember last year's rumors about Miss?"
Not a confession. Deflated, Hongdou muttered, "Of course. Why bring up ancient history?"
Checking the alley was empty, Asheng whispered, "A servant from Eldest Young Master's yard told me today that our own young master started those rumors."
Disappointment turned to shock. "What? Second Young Master spread them?"
"Keep your voice down!"
"What do we do?" Hongdou fretted. "Poor Miss—she hated marrying him already! If she learns he wrecked her match with Young Master Qiao with those lies, she'll be crushed. Yet leaving her in the dark like a fool is pitiful too!"
"Exactly! Do we tell her or not? I'll follow your lead."
"I have no idea..."
"What are you two whispering about in the corner?" a crisp voice cut in.
Spinning around, they saw Matron Wei, just back from checking the shops. Exchanging a relieved glance—Matron Wei always knew best—both bowed. "Matron, please step inside your room," Hongdou urged. "Asheng and I have something urgent to report."
Inside Matron Wei's quarters, before she could even sit, the pair poured out the whole story.
Matron Wei sank onto her couch in disbelief. Sharp as she was, she had never guessed the groom was the culprit behind last year's scandal.
Then every piece clicked into place. When the betrothal was struck last year, she could understand the Chens overlooking a mutual divorce, yet brushing off citywide slander had baffled her. Now it all made sense. Prefect Zhu cared fiercely about face and had once been heard by Madam Xiang investigating the rumormonger. Suddenly the probe went silent, followed by a rushed match with the Chen household. Prefect Zhu had caught the culprit and forced the marriage—convinced he had saved Zhu face while securing a wealthy husband for his daughter, leaving his girl completely in the dark.
"Run along, both of you," Matron Wei said. "Let me think this through."
"Yes, Matron." Both stepped out, relieved. Asheng exhaled. "Handing that headache to Matron Wei takes a ton off my chest."
Still annoyed over her misread romantic hopes, Hongdou snapped, "Enjoy your relief then—I've got chores!"
Asheng blinked at her marching back. "What a weird mood swing—she was fine a second ago!"
#CH 223
#TITLE: The Culprit Is the Groom Himself
Should she tell her young mistress that the groom had started last year's rumors? Matron Wei sat at the edge of her couch, weighing the odds.
Keep quiet, and since even servants were talking, Miss would learn sooner or later. Tell her, and fresh venom would poison whatever peace remained between husband and wife.
Her mind drifted back to running into Yao Qingyan in the manor garden earlier that afternoon.
On her way back from running errands, Yingxue had called out to her from a garden pavilion where Yao Qingyan sat resting and beckoning with a warm smile. Guessing the mistress had waited there to intercept her, Matron Wei had detoured over, curtsied, and taken a stone stool.
"I wanted to thank you, Matron," Yao Qingyan had said, "for helping Shuzhen—and helping me in the process."
"Forgive me, Madam, which matter do you mean?"
"You've helped her so much you can't keep track! Winning over Old Madam Xia."
"Ah—I only dropped a passing hint. Credit goes to Miss for taking it to heart and acting on it."
"A sharp matron and a thoughtful young lady," Yao Qingyan praised, before her brow furrowed. "There's another headache I need your clever mind on."
"What troubles you, Madam?"
"Haoyu and Shuzhen. Married, yet unconsummated, living separate lives—him roaming outside all day, her ignoring his existence. Heaven knows if I'll ever hold a chubby grandson."
Matron Wei had expected this day to come; some clauses of a prenuptial pact could hold in Chen Manor, others could not. "Don't rush, Madam. Take it slow."
"True enough. Set grandsons aside for now—first we need to rein Haoyu in. Old Madam Xia, Jianglin, and I talked it over and want Shuzhen in charge of disciplining him. We asked her before, and she nodded politely without lifting a finger. We can't very well nag her again, so I'm begging you to figure out a way to make Shuzhen rein him in of her own free will."
Now Matron Wei saw why Yao Qingyan had ambushed her in the pavilion. "Raising sons is usually the elders' job. Never heard of a new bride being tasked with educating her own husband."
"You're right, and as his mother I blush to ask it," Yao Qingyan admitted. "Yet Old Madam Xia, Jianglin, and I turned it over and saw huge upside—above all, if she disciplines him, they'll clash every day. Knock two stubborn rocks together long enough and sparks fly, let alone two flesh-and-blood people! Wouldn't you agree?"
Matron Wei found the scheme almost funny, yet understandable: Old Madam Xia spoiled him too much to strike hard, Yao Qingyan lacked the stomach, and Chen Jianglin's firm hand went nowhere while both women shielded the boy. Shuzhen was the ideal enforcer—the elders got peace, family harmony stayed intact, and if Shuzhen reformed Haoyu, the Chens gained a worthy son and maybe a warm marriage to boot. Even Matron Wei saw no downside to her mistress shaping a decent husband—except that Miss honored her non-interference pact to the letter.
"Clever idea, Madam, only I doubt Miss will agree."
"That's why I'm begging you!" Yao Qingyan had risen and started sinking toward her knees. "If you don't say yes, I'll kneel right here until you do!"
Horrified—no mistress knelt to a servant—Matron Wei caught her arms and held her upright. "You'll shorten my life doing that, Madam! I'll accept the task, though I can't promise Miss will agree—only that I'll try my best."
Yao Qingyan had beamed and squeezed her hands. "With you on the case, we're as good as done!"
Back in her room, Matron Wei connected the dots.
If she told her mistress the truth, Miss would fly into a rage and refuse to let the groom off the hook—ending his carefree days overnight. Even if she acted out of revenge rather than duty, the result was discipline all the same. Knowing her mistress's heart, tough as her fists were, she would never maim or kill him, only put him through the wringer—and heaven knew that scoundrel had it coming.
Matron Wei did not expect love overnight, yet she wanted a solid husband by her mistress's side. Looking at Chen Jianglin's devotion to his wife, Haoyu had good clay in his bones. If one day he treated Shuzhen half as well as his father treated Yao Qingyan, Matron Wei would smile in her sleep.
Decision made, she stepped outside, glanced across the back courtyard at Boya Study, and murmured, "She already banished the groom back here to live across from me—what can't she handle? Helping her whip up a worthy husband is nothing to hesitate over."
Inside Suxin Thatched Hall, Qianli Xun was writing fresh pages.
